title: Synthesis of Cu2O Nanostructures with Tunable Crystal Facets for Electrochemical CO2 Reduction to Alcohols
abstract: Electrochemical CO2 reduction enables the conversion of intermittent renewable energy to value-added chemicals and fuel, presenting a promising strategy to relieve CO2 emission and achieve clean energy storage. In this work, we developed nanosized Cu2O catalysts using the hydrothermal method for electrochemical CO2 reduction to alcohols. Cu2O nanoparticles (NPs) of various morphologies that were enclosed with different crystal facets, named as Cu2O-c (cubic structure with (100) facets), Cu2O-o (octahedron structure with (111) facets), Cu2O-t (truncated octahedron structure with both (100) and (111) facets), and Cu2O-u (urchin-like structure with (100), (220), and (222) facets), were prepared by regulating the content of a polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP) template. The electrochemical CO2 reduction performance of the different Cu2O NPs was evaluated in the CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte. The as-synthesized Cu2O nanostructures were capable of reducing CO2 to produce alcohols including methanol, ethanol, and isopropanol. The alcohol selectivity of the different Cu2O NPs followed the order of Cu2O-t < Cu2O-u < Cu2O-c < Cu2O-o (with the total Faradaic efficiencies of alcohol products of 10.7, 25.0, 26.2, and 35.4%). The facet-dependent effects were associated with the varied concentrations of oxygen-vacancy defects, different energy barriers of CO2 reduction, and distinct Cu−O bond lengths over the different crystal facets. The desired Cu2O-o catalyst exhibited good reduction activity with the highest partial current density of 0.51 mA/cm for alcohols. The Faradaic efficiencies of alcohol products were 4.9% for methanol, 17.9% for ethanol, and 12.6% for isopropanol. The good electrochemical CO2 reduction performance was also associated with the surface reconstruction of Cu2O, which endowed the catalyst with abundant Cu and Cu sites for promoted CO2 activation and stabilized CO* adsorption for enhanced C−C coupling. This work will provide a new route for enhancing the alcohol selectivity of nanostructured Cu2O catalysts by crystal facet engineering.

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Rapid depletion of fossil fuels has resulted in the severe global warming and energy crisis.1 As fossil fuels will remain the dominant position in the global energy system from a nearterm perspective, intensive CO2 emissions will continue contributing to global warming and climate change. Carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) has been perceived as a promising strategy to mitigate CO2 emissions.
2,3 Nevertheless, the large-scale deployment of CCUS projects has been hindered by their high cost and great energy consumption. Renewable energy also plays an important role in CO2 emission reduction with respect to energy structure alterations. However, the large-scale application of renewable energy has been limited by its intermittent characteristics. Taking all of these into account, CCUS powered by renewable energy could be one innovative concept. Executing the scheme of CCUS
integrated with renewable energy has a double functionality to achieve CO2 emission reduction and clean energy storage. 4,5
One typical technical route of CCUS integrated with renewable energy is the electrochemical CO2 reduction (ECR) to value-added chemicals and fuels.2,6 Depending on the multiple-electron transfer pathways, the products of ECR include CO,7−9 methane,10 ethylene,11 formic acid,12−14 methanol,15−17 ethanol,18−20 and other C2+ alcohols. 21 Among them, alcohols are represented as desired products that have gained widespread attention, as they could be

employed as an important medium in future energy systems and essential intermediates in chemical synthesis. ECR to alcohols (CH3OH, C2H6O, and C3H8O) can be performed under ambient conditions through 6-electron, 12-electron, and 18-electron transfer pathways.22 Thermodynamically, the potential for CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) is 20 mV, which is positive compared to that for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), and thus, the competition between CO2RR and HER results in low selectivity toward alcohols.23 This remains a significant challenge for the efficient reduction of CO2 to alcohols. For this cause, an electrocatalyst plays a significant role in improving the selectivity of alcohols and suppressing HER.24
Cuprous oxide (Cu2O) is one of the typical electrocatalysts that shows promise for ECR to alcohols.23 However, Cu2O is also faced with the issues of poor reduction activity and low alcohol selectivity. Efforts have been devoted to doping Cu2O with a second monoatomic metal or metal oxide for enriched oxygen vacancy and therefore will promote CO2 activation for improved electrochemical performance.25−27 To solve the problem of insufficient catalyst activity and low target product selectivity, one of the promising approaches is tuning the surface morphology and crystal structure of Cu2O. The surface of metal oxides generally presents a more complex crystal structure and surface morphology than metals. Model catalysts with uniform and well-defined surface structures have been extensively employed to explore structure−property relationships of powder catalysts. For metal oxide catalysts, the crystal facets exposed on the metal oxide particles not only determine the surface geometry but also strongly influence the catalytic performance.28 Special consideration should therefore be given to crystal facets while designing efficient catalysts for ECR to alcohols. In addition, it is also essential to gain an in-depth understanding of how crystal facets affect the reduction activity and alcohol selectivity of Cu2O in the ECR process. Cu2O nanocrystals enclosed with different crystal planes (such as (100), (110), and (111) facets) have been fabricated for ethylene production from the electrochemical reduction of CO2. The products of ECR over Cu2O nanostructures depend on the varied crystal planes, as crystal facets will decide the active sites for stabilizing important intermediates in product formation. For example, the (111) facet of Cu is conducive to the preferential formation of CH4, while the (100) facet of Cu and some high-index crystal facets (such as (200) and (220) facets) are favorable for C−C coupling to form C2H4. Gao et al. also confirmed that the activity and selectivity of C2H4 production depended on the crystal facets in Cu2O nanostructures. The Cu2O nanoparticles (NPs) enclosed with both (100) and (111) facets were capable of electrochemically reducing CO2 to C2H4 with a high Faradaic efficiency of 59%.29 In the work by Wu et al., the (110) facets in Cu2O had been demonstrated to be photocatalytically active for CO2 reduction to methanol, and the Cu2O NPs containing (110) facets worked satisfactorily with a great internal quantum yield of 72%.30 Definitely, the facet-dependent mechanisms for CO2 reduction over Cu2O NPs to produce C2H4 and methanol could be different. To date, the facetdependent effect on the CO2 reduction activity and alcohol selectivity of Cu2O nanostructures remains unknown, and identifying the key crystal facets for promoted alcohol production is critically essential. As a result, we have developed Cu2O nanostructures with different crystal facets, named as Cu2O-c (cubic structure
enclosed with (100) facets), Cu2O-o (octahedron structure enclosed with (111) facets), Cu2O-t (truncated octahedron structure enclosed with both (100) and (111) facets), and Cu2O-u (urchin-like structure with (211) and (111) facets) for ECR to alcohols. The objective of the work is to disclose the facet-dependent effect on the ECR performance of Cu2O nanostructures for alcohol production. The results will certainly provide insightful guidance for designing highly efficient Cu2O catalysts for ECR application by regulating their crystal facets.

sections.heading: 2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
sections.text:
2.1. Materials and Catalyst Preparation. Nanosized Cu2O catalysts were prepared using a template-assisted hydrothermal synthesis process. Copper chloride dihydrate (CuCl2·2H2O) and copper nitrate (Cu(NO3)2) were employed as precursors. Polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP,Mw = 24,000) and D-(+)-glucose were employed as a template and reducing agent, respectively.30,31
2.1.1. Synthesis of Cu2O with Regular Surface Morphology. A certain gram of PVP was added into 100 mL of CuCl2·2H2O aqueous solution (0 g of PVP for Cu2O-c, 4 g of PVP for Cu2O-o, and 6 g of PVP for Cu2O-t), followed by addition of 10 mL of NaOH (2 M) dropwise into the mixture. Sky blue precipitates were first observed in the solution, and then the precipitates gradually turned black, accompanied by the production of black flocculent precipitation. After constant stirring for 30 min, 1.2 g of D-(+)-glucose was added into the solution. The color of the liquid changed gradually from black to turbid red. The total volume of the solution was 110 mL. The mixture was aged for 3 h, all the procedures were carried out under constant vigorous stirring, and the mixture was heated at 60 °C. The resulting precipitate was collected by centrifugation at 5000 rpm. For 3 min, followed by washing with distilled water two times and absolute ethanol two times and, finally, drying under vacuum at 60 °C for 6 h. The specific procedures for synthesizing Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o, and Cu2O-t are presented in Figure S1a.
2.1.2. Synthesis of Cu2O-u. A total of 1.208 g of Cu(NO3)2 was dissolved in 50 mL of deionized water and stirred well until it was completely dissolved. Then, 5 mL of NaOH (6 M) was added dropwise into the above solution. After stirring for 5 min, the color of the solution gradually turned into black under the hydrothermal conditions. Afterward, 0.8 g of D-(+)-glucose was added into the above solution. All the procedures were heated at 98 °C with constant vigorous stirring. The resulting precipitate was collected by centrifugation at 5000 rpm for 3 min, washed with deionized water twice and absolute ethanol twice, and finally dried under vacuum at 60 °C for 6 h. The specific procedures for synthesizing Cu2O-u are shown in Figure S1b.
2.1.3. Synthesis of Bulk Cu and CuO. For the sake of comparison, bulk Cu and CuO catalysts were also prepared using the similar methods reported in the literature. Cu foil (5 cm × 5 cm) was electropolished in 200 mL of 85% phosphoric acid for 1 h and then annealed in a N2 atmosphere at 300 °C for 3 h to obtain the desired bulk Cu.32 CuO was prepared by calcining the Cu2O-o catalysts at 350 °C in a tube furnace for 30 min to obtain the desired CuO sample.11
2.2. Preparation of the Working Electrodes. Typically, an ink of Cu2O, Cu, or CuO particles was prepared by mixing 20 mg of catalyst (Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o, Cu2O-t, Cu2O-u, bulk Cu, and CuO) with 40 μL of 5% Nafion solution and 80 μL of deionized water. The ink was sonicated in an ultrasonic cleaner for 30 min. The collected ink was then uniformly coated on the surface of carbon paper electrode with a geometric size of 1 cm × 1 cm to form a thin protective film and then dried under an infrared lamp. Finally, the well-prepared electrode was used for the ECR tests.
2.3. Characterization. Crystalline structures of the samples were identified by X-ray diffraction analysis (XRD, Bruker D8 Advance, Germany). Surface morphologies were investigated by field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, JSM-7800F Prime, Japan)

Chemical valences of the catalysts were identified by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo ESCALAB 250xi, America). 2.4. Electrochemical CO2 Reduction Test. The electrochemical performance of the catalysts was evaluated in a three-electrode H-type cell using the prepared Cu2O samples as the working electrode, Ag/ AgCl as the reference electrode (filled with saturated KCl), and the platinum mesh electrode as the counter electrode (Figure S2). The anode and cathode chambers of the H-type cell were separated by a proton exchange membrane. Linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV) and cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements were carried out in N2- and CO2-saturated KHCO3 electrolytes (0.5 M, pH ≈ 8.45) under the potential of −0.3 to −1.6 V vs Ag/AgCl (for LSV) and 0.5 to −1.6 V vs Ag/AgCl (for CV). sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
The as-synthesized Cu2O electrocatalysts were characterized by different techniques. Figure 1 shows that the XRD patterns
of the different Cu2O NPs represent diffraction peaks associated with crystalline Cu2O (PDF#05-0667) in the wide 2θ range of 29.18° to 77.84°.39 The average crystal sizes of the different Cu2O nanostructures are calculated using the Scherrer formula. They are 55.51, 56.64, 51.74, and 56.53 nm for Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o, Cu2O-t, and Cu2O-u, respectively. The strong intensity and narrow width of the peak centered at 36.42° indicate the good crystallinity of the as-synthesized Cu2O catalysts. In addition, the (111) peak intensity of the Cu2O-u catalyst is higher than those of Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o, and Cu2O-t catalysts. This is because Cu2O-u is synthesized under hydrothermal conditions of a relatively higher water-bath
https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.1c03850 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2021, 13, 39165−39177
39167
temperature (98 °C) and high-concentration NaOH solution (6 M), and these will facilitate the rapid nucleation of Cu2O. Figure 2 shows the SEM images of the different Cu2O catalysts. As expected, the as-synthesized Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o,
Cu2O-t, and Cu2O-u nanostructures exhibit the desired cubic, octahedron, truncated octahedron, and sea urchin-like morphologies. In detail, the Cu2O-c catalyst is composed of (100) crystal facets, and the crystallinity of each crystal plane is excellent. In addition, the sample shows uniform particle size distribution. Similarly, the Cu2O-o catalyst is composed of (111) facets and the Cu2O-t catalyst is composed of (100) and (111) facets. The different morphologies are associated with the varied PVP contents in the hydrothermal process. The added PVP in the hydrothermal process will change the nucleation paths, thus yielding Cu2O catalysts with different crystal facets. Cu2O-u exhibits an irregular block morphology with a large number of dendritic nanorods gathered on the surface. The sea urchin-like Cu2O-u catalyst primarily consists of high-index crystal facets such as (222) and (220). The sea urchin-like morphology is associated with the fast nucleation of Cu2O under the high temperature and high-concentration NaOH solution. The different morphologies and crystal planes in the various Cu2O nanostructures might affect their ECR performance.40
To further reveal the microstructure characteristics of the different Cu2O catalysts, their TEM images are presented in Figure 3, and the HRTEM and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) images are presented in Figure S3. TEM images show the cubic, octahedron, truncated octahedron, and sea urchin-like morphologies for Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o, Cu2O-t, and Cu2O-u, respectively. The (100) facets are clearly visible on the TEM image of Cu2O-c, while the Cu2O-o catalyst is enclosed with (111) facets. Both the (100) and (111) facets can be identified for Cu2O-t. The lattice fringes with different d-spacing values in HRTEM images and the diffraction rings in the SAED images also confirm the presence of the abovementioned crystal facets. The crystal facets of Cu2O-u cannot be identified from its TEM image due to the complicated crystal structure. The HRTEM and SAED images of Cu2O-u indicate that the Cu2O-u catalyst contains at least three different crystal planes, namely, the (100), (220), and (222) crystal planes. In addition, the edge lengths of the crystal
planes for the different Cu2O nanostructures are measured as 1.37, 1.80, 1.01, and 0.55 μm. XPS analysis is performed to identify the chemical valence
states of the different Cu2O catalysts. The survey scan in Figure 4a shows the presence of Cu 2p, O 1s, and C 1s spectra. The high-resolution XPS spectra of Cu 2p are presented in Figure 4b. For the different Cu2O catalysts, two characteristic peaks with binding energy separation of around 20.0 eV can be resolved at 932.6 and 952.4 eV, which are assigned to Cu+ 2p3/2 and Cu + 2p1/2, respectively. The presence of satellite peaks at the binding energies of 945.8 and 943.1 eV should also indicate that Cu(I) is the major valance state for Cu species.41 In addition, characteristic peaks of low intensity can also be resolved at 934.8 and 954.8 eV, which are associated with Cu2+ 2p1/2 and Cu
2+ 2p3/2, respectively, indicating that a small quantity of CuO exists in the Cu2O nanostructures. The present Cu(II) is due to the oxidation of Cu(I), since Cu2O is thermodynamically unstable under normal conditions. Particularly, the characteristic peaks of Cu2+ 2p1/2 and Cu
2+ 2p3/2 for the Cu2O-u catalyst are clearly visible.
42 This is because the Cu2O-u catalyst was fabricated in the hydrothermal system with a high water-bath temperature (98 °C) and highconcentration NaOH solution (6 M). This will create an oxidizing environment for the partial oxidation of Cu2O crystals to CuO. To further distinguish Cu(I) and Cu(0), the Cu LM2 spectra are provided in Figure 4c. The Cu LM2 Auger spectra show a characteristic peak at the binding energy of 570.0 eV, which confirms that Cu(I) is the major chemical valance for Cu species. In addition, a shoulder peak corresponding to Cu(II) can also be observed at 569.3 eV, which also indicates that Cu2O has been partially oxidized, and the small quantities of oxidized CuO species can hardly be detected in the XRD patterns.39 Figure 4d depicts the highresolution O 1s spectra of the different Cu2O catalysts. The two characteristic peaks resolved at the binding energies of 530.2 and 531.6 eV are assigned to lattice oxygen (Olat) and oxygen vacancies (OVs), respectively.42,43
Surface chemical compositions of the different Cu2O nanostructures are summarized in Table 1. The surface
https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.1c03850 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2021, 13, 39165−39177
39168
compositions of the different Cu2O catalysts can be clearly distinguished by XPS analysis. The results of quantitative analysis also indicate that Cu(I) is the major chemical state for copper species. The Cu2O-c catalyst possesses a much higher Cu(I) content than the other Cu2O nanostructures. In addition, Cu(II) also accounts for 5.68−20.45% in the copper species, as an indication of the partial oxidation of Cu2O for the different catalysts. Huang et al. pointed out that the (100) crystal plane would provide the Cu2O nanostructure a more stable Cu−O bond compared to the (111) and (110) crystal planes.40 Thus, the relatively higher Cu(I) content in Cu2O-c should be ascribed to the stable Cu−O bond due to the enriched (100) crystal facets. In contrast, the unstable Cu−O bonds on the (111) and (110) planes are prone to getting broken and will therefore create active Cu(I) ions, and the dissociative Cu(I) ions are easily oxidized at room temperature. This is the reason why Cu2O-o and Cu2O-t possess relatively lower Cu(I) contents. It is worth noting that Cu2O-u suffers the most severe partial oxidation, as evidenced by the highest Cu(II) content. Apart from the unstable Cu−O bonds on the high-index crystal planes, the unique oxidizing conditions of high water-bath temperature and high-concentration NaOH solution in hydrothermal synthesis should also contribute to the severe partial oxidation of Cu2O. The O 1s atomic contents of the different Cu2O nanostructures show a
similar sequence to their Cu 2p atomic contents. Notably, the OVs/Olat ratios of Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o, and Cu2O-t are approximately 1.0, while the OVs/Olat ratio of Cu2O-u is only 0.66. The relatively lower OV content in Cu2O-u is associated with the severe partial oxidation of Cu2O. Although the dissociation of Cu−O bond in Cu2O will create abundant OVs, the subsequent Cu−O reconstruction to form CuO has resulted in the transformation of OV defects to lattice oxygen.40 Yao et al. reported that the CuO nanostructure would be partially reduced to Cu2O and metallic Cu during electrochemical CO2 reduction to syngas. A comparison of the surface chemical compositions of the fresh and spent CuO catalysts indicated that the conversion of Cu(II) to Cu(I) and Cu(0) would result in the increase in OV content by about 10%.35 In other words, the partial oxidation of Cu(I) to Cu(II) might give rise to the decrease in OVs accordingly. This might also explain why the OV concentration of Cu2O-u is much lower than those of the other three catalysts. Some previous contributions indicate that OVs played important roles in promoting electron transfer and adsorption on metal oxide catalysts. 126.97, 160.23, and 207.85 μF/cm2 for Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o, Cu2O-t, and Cu2O-u, respectively. Their ECSA values are then determined as 3.29, 3.17, 4.01, and 5.20 cm2, respectively. LSV and CV tests were conducted in the CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte under the applied potentials of −1.0 to 0.5 V vs RHE and 0.59 to 0.66 V vs RHE. The ECSA-normalized LSV and CV curves are shown in Figure 6. The LSV curves show that the onset potentials decrease in the order of Cu2O-o > Cu2O-u > Cu2O-t > Cu2O-c, which means that the Cu2O-o catalyst has the most negative onset potential and the highest reduction activity. Similarly, the CV curves reveal the best reduction activity of the Cu2O-o catalyst with the normalized current density up to −6.5 mA/cm2 under the applied potential of −0.30 V vs RHE. Two obvious reduction peaks can be observed under the potentials of −0.30 and 0.40 V vs RHE, corresponding to CO2RR and HER. In addition, CV curves of the different Cu2O catalysts tested in the N2saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte are shown in Figure S5. CV curves of the Cu2O catalysts tested in the N2-saturated electrolyte exhibit an oxidation peak in −0.2 to 0.2 V vs RHE, indicating that the Cu2O catalysts have been partially oxidized. No reduction peaks can be observed under the applied potential of −0.3 to −0.9 V vs RHE. CV curves of the bulk Cu and CuO catalysts are also provided in Figure S6. The cathodic current density of the different Cu-based catalysts in the N2saturated electrolyte is associated with the HER process, while the cathodic current density in the CO2-saturated electrolyte
corresponds to the CO2RR process. For bulk Cu and Cu2O-o catalysts, the cathodic current densities in the presence and absence of CO2 are close, indicating that the HER and CO2RR processes compete with each other. In contrast, the CuO catalyst shows a much higher current density in the CO2saturated electrolyte than that in the N2-saturated electrolyte, indicating that CO2RR prevails over HER. Moreover, an obvious reduction peak can be observed on the CV curves of all the catalysts tested in the CO2-saturated electrolyte, corresponding to the different reduction products in CO2RR. An electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) study
was performed to evaluate the charge transfer resistance of the different catalysts. As charge transfer resistance is the major barrier that needs to be overcome, the impedance of the diffusion is negligible. The equivalent circuit model that corresponds to the charge transfer control mechanism is employed to correlate the EIS data in the charge transfer control region. The fitted plots of Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o, Cu2O-t, and Cu2O-u and the equivalent circuit model are displayed in Figure 7. In addition, the fitted plots of bulk Cu and CuO are
also provided in Figure S7.44 The results in Table S1 indicate that the fitting error is less than 20%, and the corresponding values of Rct are 690.4, 480.5, 2054, and 533.8 Ω for Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o, Cu2O-t, and Cu2O-u catalysts, respectively. This indicates that Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o, and Cu2O-u exhibit lower impedance for charge transfer, and the smaller charge transfer resistance would result in a favorable Faradaic process. The stability of the Cu2O catalysts in ECR is an important factor that needed to be considered in practical application.

The stability of the different Cu2O catalysts in long-term CO2 reduction tests was evaluated under the potential of −0.3 V vs RHE. Figure 8 shows that the different Cu2O nanostructures
keep good working stability with the continuous bubbling of CO2 into the KHCO3 electrolyte. Particularly, the Cu2O-o catalyst retains a high and constant ECSA-normalized current density of −1.47 mA/cm2 for about 400 min, indicating that the catalyst maintains stable ECR performance in the longterm test. Faradaic efficiencies (FEs) and ECSA-normalized partial
current densities of the products of the different catalysts under −0.3 V vs RHE are shown in Figure 9. The detected gaseous products involve H2, CO, and CH4 and the liquid products include formate, methanol, ethanol, and isopropanol. The total FEs of the different Cu2O nanostructures are 78.8, 97.3, 58.3, and 56.8% for Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o, Cu2O-t, and Cu2O-u, respectively. The total FEs of bulk Cu and CuO are 96.3 and 18.4%, respectively. As indicated in Figure 9a, the different Cu2O nanostructures favor the formation of CO with high FEs, while the low FEs for H2 should imply that the HER has been suppressed. This indicates that the Cu2O catalysts are capable of activating CO2 to form CO* intermediates, while the surfaces of the catalysts are not expected to stabilize the key CO* intermediates or fail to overcome more energy barriers to absorb electrons for further C−C coupling to form C2+ products. For the liquid products, the Cu2O-c and Cu2O-o catalysts favor the formation of ethanol and isopropanol. In contrast, methanol and isopropanol are the desired liquid products for Cu2O-t and
Cu2O-u, respectively. The total FEs of the liquid alcohols are 26.2, 35.4, 10.7, and 25.0% for Cu2O-c, Cu2O-o, Cu2O-t, and Cu2O-u, respectively. Notably, Cu2O-o exhibits the best alcohol selectivity in the ECR process. In addition, the total FEs of the liquid alcohols are 70.2 and 17.0% for bulk Cu and CuO, respectively. The desired Cu2O-o catalyst shows a higher alcohol selectivity than CuO, while the total FEs of alcohols are still far from that of bulk Cu. Figure 9b shows the ECSAnormalized partial current densities of the products of the different Cu2O catalysts. The desired Cu2O-o catalyst shows high ECSA-normalized partial current densities for both the gaseous and liquid products. The ECSA-normalized partial current densities of Cu2O for methanol, ethanol and isopropanol are 0.07, 0.26, and 0.18 mA/cm2, respectively, which are higher than that of bulk Cu and CuO. This also indicates that the desired Cu2O-o exhibits higher activity for generating alcohols against others in the ECR process. To gain a better understanding of the kinetics of CO2 reduction over the different catalysts, their Tafel plots for alcohol products are shown in Figure S8. The Tafel slopes of bulk Cu for producing methanol, ethanol, and isopropanol are as high as 356 mV/dec, which indicates that bulk Cu shows poor kinetics in ECR. The Tafel slopes of Cu2O-o are 102, 94, and 94 mV/dec for methanol, ethanol, and isopropanol, respectively, which are the lowest among the different catalysts. This indicates that Cu2O-o exhibits intrinsically better activity and faster kinetics for electrochemical CO2 reduction. The difference in reduction activity and alcohol selectivity of
the different Cu2O nanostructures is associated with their OV concentrations and crystal facets. It is widely acknowledged that the ECR process over copper-based catalysts involves several steps: the adsorption and activation of CO2 on the specific facets to form CO2 −, the transformation of CO2 − to CO* intermediates and the stabilization of the intermediates on the surface, and C−C coupling of the adjacent CO* intermediates via electron or proton transfer or loss of oxygen atoms to generate different products.45,46 CO2 adsorption and activation and the stabilization of intermediates have been reported depending on OV concentrations and crystal facets. Oxygen-vacancy defects played important roles in promoting
the adsorption and activation of CO2 on metal oxide catalysts in the ECR process. Gao et al. reported that the oxygen(II) vacancy was the main defect in cobalt oxide for ECR to formate. As proton transfer was the rate-limiting step, oxygen(II) vacancies worked satisfactorily in lowering the rate-limiting activation barrier by stabilizing the formate anion radical intermediate. The OV-rich and OV-poor catalysts
https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.1c03850 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2021, 13, 39165−39177
39171
therefore exhibited distinct maximum FEs of 87.6 and 67.3% for formate production under −0.87 V vs SCE, respectively.47 Geng et al. confirmed that the inclusion of oxygen vacancies increased the charge density of the ZnO catalyst, and this further facilitated CO2 activation by enhancing the binding strength of CO2. The OV-rich ZnO nanosheets exhibited high activity (jCO = −16.1 mA/cm2) and excellent selectivity (FECO = 83%) for ECR to CO production.48 It has also been reported that both the surface and bulk OVs in nanostructured metal oxides played vital roles in gas adsorption and activation.43 Our experimental results indicate that Cu2O-o possesses the best reduction activity and alcohol selectivity. XPS analysis implies that the Cu2O-o catalyst possesses the highest OVs/Olat ratio, which evidences that the good ECR performance should be associated with the enriched oxygen-vacancy defects. Considering the important roles of OVs, strategies including thermal annealing and metal oxide doping have been widely employed to increase the concentration of OVs in metal oxide catalysts for promoted catalytic performance.26,27,49
Crystal facets also play pivotal roles in deciding the selectivity of the desired products in ECR. The activation barriers for the adsorption of proton-electron pair and the dimerization and trimerization of the intermediates over the different crystal facets could be different, corresponding to the different ECR pathways and varied products. Gao et al. and Fu et al. highlighted the crystal facet-dependent effect of Cu2O on the performance of ECR to C2H4 and C2+ products.
29,50 DFT calculations by Gao et al. indicated that the (100) and joint (100)/(111) facets showed much stronger binding strength toward CO* intermediates than the (111) facet. This implied that the (100) and joint (100)/(111) facets favored C−C coupling to produce C2+ products. In addition, the C2H4 product could be adsorbed more strongly on the (100) facet than the (100) and joint (100)/(111) facets. In other words, C2H4 could hardly escape from the (100) facet.
29 Nevertheless, Fu et al. considered (111) and other high-index facets as highly active for C2+ production. The Cu2O-o catalyst enclosed by (111) and other high-index facets exhibited a high C2+ selectivity of 48.3% under −1.1 V vs RHE.50 Reconstruction and fragmentation occurred more quickly over Cu2O-o, and more crystal defects were available for CO2 reduction. Hence, the high-index facets and the abundant active sites derived from surface reconstruction contributed to the improved C−C coupling.50 It is worth noting that mechanistic pathways of CO2 reduction to C2H4 and alcohol products over copperbased catalysts could be different. Both the (100) and (111) facets favor C−C coupling via the dimerization of the adjacent adsorbed CO* molecules. A further reduction of C2O2* on the (100) facet via proton transfer corresponds the formation of C2H4. Therefore, the high CO* coverage on the (100) facet reduces the energy barrier for CO* dimerization to produce

45 In contrast, the high CO* coverage on the (111) facet will decrease the C−C coupling energy barrier. With the increase in CO* coverage on the (111) facet, the reaction energy associated with the conversion of C2O2H* and C3O2H* to C2+ alcohols would decrease more than that associated with C2H4 formation via the CCH* intermediate. 46 This has also been evidenced by the DFT calculation results reported in an open document. Hence, the (111) facet reduces the energy barrier for C−C coupling and transformation of the key intermediates and promotes electron migration for alcohol production.
The catalytic activity of the Cu2O nanostructures has also been correlated to the surface composition and the structure of exposed crystal planes. Copper-based catalysts involve different crystal facets, which correspond to various Cu−O bonds. The ECR process should overcome the kinetic barrier to break the different surface Cu−O bonds. DFT modeling indicated that the bond lengths of Cu−O bonds on the (100), (110), and (111) crystal planes are 1.76, 1.82, and 1.83 Å, respectively.40 Hence, the Cu2O (100) surface with the shortest surface Cu− O bond is more stable than the (110) and (111) planes. In other words, the kinetic barrier could be higher for the proceeding of ECR over the (100) facet.40 One can well perceive that the Cu2O-o catalyst enclosed with (111) facets exhibits relatively lower charge transfer resistance, which also confirms that the kinetic barrier that needs to be overcome on (111) facets could be lower. This should also be associated with the facilitated CO2 reduction process over the desired Cu2O-o catalyst. To gain more detailed insights into the selectivity for
CO2RR to alcohols on the Cu2O nanostructures, DFT calculations were performed to explore the change in free energy in the CO2RR process. Figure 10 shows the schematic
representations of intermediates and products involved in the pathways to alcohols in the ECR process.45 The key intermediates identified for the CH3OH, C2H6O, and C3H8O products are CHO*, C2O2H*, and C3O2H*, respectively. The different key intermediates are obtained by the adsorption of multiple protons and electrons or the dimerization and/or trimerization of CO*. Free energies of the intermediates are determined via DFT calculations using the CASTEP program in Materials Studio. We employ generalized
https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.1c03850 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2021, 13, 39165−39177
39172
gradient approximation (GGA) of the Perdew−Burke− Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation functional and a cutoff energy of 500 eV. A customized 3 × 3 × 1 k-point grid is adopted for calculation.51 Detailed descriptions of the DFT calculations can be found in the Supporting Information. Figure 11 shows the free energy profiles for CO2RR to alcohols on the Cu2O nanostructures through the CHO*-, C2O2H*-, and C3O2H*-generating pathways. Our DFT calculation results in Figure 11 and Figures S9−S11 show that the free energies of CO2* on the (100), (110), and (111) facets of Cu2O are −0.68, −0.23, and −0.78 eV, respectively. This implies that the (111) facet favors CO2 adsorption and activation. Our characterization results prove that the Cu2O-o catalyst enclosed by the (111) facet contains massive OVs, which will also be conducive to further lowering the energy barrier for CO2 adsorption and activation. As shown in Figure 11, the free energies of the CO* intermediate on (111), (100), and (110) facets are −0.36, −0.25, and −0.30 eV, respectively. CO* is more strongly adsorbed on the (111) facet than on the (100) facet and (110) facet. This indicates that the (111) facet favors the adsorption and stabilization of the CO* intermediate, and this will subsequently facilitate C−C coupling to produce C2+ products during the ECR process.29 This is in good agreement with the higher FEs toward alcohol production of the Cu2O-o catalyst enclosed by the (111) facet. It should also be noticed that the applied potential of −0.3 to −0.9 eV is insufficient to stabilize all the CO* intermediates. Thus, a portion of CO* will be transformed to CO and escape from the catalyst surface, as evidenced by the relatively high FE toward CO formation on Cu2O-o. The CHO*, C2O2H*, and C3O2H* intermediates can be formed from CO* by the different proton-coupled electron transfer processes, and their generating pathways correspond to the alcohols of methanol, ethanol, and isopropanol, respectively. In addition, the free energies of the different key intermediates on the (111), (100), and (110) facets are different. The CHO* and C2O2H* intermediates show negative free energies on the (111) facet. In contrast, the C3O2H* intermediate shows a positive free energy, implying that the protonation of CO*-coupled electron transfer process needs extra energy to trigger. Hence, the (111) facet favors the
formation of methanol and ethanol. This conforms well to the selectivity of the alcohol products on Cu2O-o. For the (100) facet, the CHO*, C2O2H*, and C3O2H* intermediates all show negative free energies, and the values for C2O2H* and C3O2H* are more negative. Hence, the (100) facet might be favorable for the formation of ethanol and isopropanol. This has also been evidenced by the much higher FEs of ethanol and isopropanol than methanol on Cu2O-c. Similarly, the (110) facet favors methanol production, while the formation of ethanol and isopropanol needs to overcome extra energy. Overall, our DFT calculations also confirm the thermodynamic feasibility of CO2 reduction to alcohols with relatively higher selectivity on Cu2O-o enclosed by the (111) facet. Surface reconstruction of Cu2O might also occur in the ECR process and this will also affect the ECR performance. The desired Cu2O-o is tested in both N2- and CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolytes under −0.3 V vs RHE. The catalysts before and after reaction are characterized by XPS analysis to study the possible structural and composition changes. The Cu 2p spectra in Figure S12a show characteristic peaks for Cu2+ 2p1/2 and Cu 2+ 2p3/2 as an indication of the partial oxidization of Cu(I). The Cu LM2 spectra in Figure S12b confirms that Cu(I) is the major chemical valance for Cu species, and no characteristic peaks for Cu(0) can be observed. Thus, it is rather difficult to evidence the surface reconstruction via the ex situ characterization technique. The in situ Raman spectra provided by Fu et al. showed that the surfaces of the Cu2O catalysts were converted to metallic Cu during CO2RR and the Cu nanoparticles (NPs) could be further re-oxidized to Cu2O NPs after the tests. Thus, quick surface reconstruction of Cu2O certainly occurs during CO2RR.
50 The surface reconstruction plays an important role in promoting the ECR performance of the Cu2O catalysts. More recently, Yuan et al. demonstrated that the Cu0-Cu+ pairs show a synergistic effect on the ECR process of Cu-based catalysts for C2H4 formation. Cu
0 sites contribute to activating CO2 and promoting electron transfers, while Cu+ sites play important roles in strengthening and stabilizing the adsorption of CO* intermediate to boost C−C coupling.52 Hence, the good activity and high alcohol selectivity of Cu2O-o might also be correlated to the Cu
0- Cu+ active sites due to surface reconstruction.

The desired Cu2O-o catalyst was further tested under the applied potentials of −0.3 to −0.9 V vs RHE. FEs of the varied products and the ECSA-normalized partial current densities are illustrated in Figure 10. The total FEs of the gaseous and liquid products are measured as 97.3, 21.4, 14.4, and 66.7% for the catalyst tested under −0.3, −0.5, −0.7, and −0.9 V vs RHE, as indicated in Figure 12a. Notably, the FEH2 of Cu2O-o is only 10.8% at −0.3 V vs RHE, indicating that a lower applied potential favors CO2RR, as most of the FEs are associated with CO and alcohols. In contrast, a higher potential favors HER of the Cu2O catalyst, as indicated by the high H2 selectivity (FEH2 = 55.9%) at −0.9 V vs RHE. As the applied potential changes from −0.3 to −0.9 V vs RHE, the total FEs of alcohol products decrease from 35.4% to 1.6%. The Cu2O-o catalyst exhibits the highest alcohol selectivity under the desired potential of −0.3 V vs RHE, as the HER process has been largely suppressed. As indicated in Figure 12b, the partial current densities for CH3OH, C2H6O, and C3H8O of the catalyst tested under −0.3 V vs RHE are in the range of 0.07 to 0.26 mA/cm2, while the CO partial current density is as high as 0.60 mA/cm2. The partial current densities of the various products are uniformly distributed under the applied potential of −0.5 V vs RHE. C2H6O is the only alcohol product for the Cu2O-o catalyst tested under −0.7 and −0.9 V vs RHE. Particularly, the Cu2Oo catalyst shows an extraordinarily high H2 partial current density of 9.99 mA/cm2 at −0.9 V vs RHE, indicating that HER dominates the ECR process under such a high applied potential. These are in good conformity with the results of FE analysis. Figure S13 shows that the Cu2O-o catalyst tested under different potentials exhibits good stability within 70 min. The stabilized ECSA-normalized current density increases with
the increasing potential from −0.3 to −0.9 V vs RHE. Although the catalyst possesses a high current density at −0.9 V vs RHE, the majority of the current densities are associated with the HER process. Overall, the Cu2O-o catalyst shows the best reduction activity and alcohol selectivity under the desired potential of −0.3 V vs RHE. The ECR performance of the Cu2O-o catalyst is compared to those of copper-based catalysts reported in open documents, and the results are summarized in Table 2. Hossain et al. reported that the Cu/TiO2 catalyst showed a very low methanol selectivity of 5% under −2.5 V vs NHE, while the catalyst showed higher selectivity toward CO and H2. The addition of TiO2 nanotubes promoted CO2 adsorption and stabilized the essential reaction intermediate and therefore afforded the Cu/TiO2 catalyst a stable ECR process.
53 To improve the ECR performance of copper-based catalysts, CuO and Cu2O had been doped with TiO2 and ZnO, respectively.54,55 The total FEs for alcohol products of CuO/ TiO2 and Cu2O/ZnO were 42.6 and 31.4%, respectively. The high activity of CuO/TiO2 in ECR was ascribed to the special roles of TiO2 in improving its CO2 adsorption capacity. 55 Doping ZnO would strengthen the Cu-CO− link and stabilize Cu species in the hydrogenation reaction and therefore would enhance the catalytic activity and alcohol selectivity of the Cu2O/ZnO catalyst. The promoted catalytic activity might also be associated with the gas diffusion electrodes and flow cell configuration for alleviated mass transport limitations.54
Periasamy et al. fabricated stable cuprous oxide/polypyrrole (Cu2O/Ppy) particles for selective CO2 reduction to methanol, and the catalyst possessed an extraordinarily high FE of 93 ± 1.2% for methanol production under −0.85 V vs RHE.56 The

pyrrolic nitrogen atoms in the Ppy shell functioned as essential active sites for CO2 molecules. In addition, the Ppy shell protected the Cu2O particles from being corroded and dissolved, and the structural and crystal facet changes could also be avoided. These endowed the Cu2O/Ppy catalyst with high selectivity and good stability.56 In this work, the desired Cu2O-o is capable of reducing CO2 under −0.3 V vs RHE in the aqueous electrolyte to promote alcohol production with a high selectivity of 35.4%. Although the FE is far from that of Cu2O/Ppy, the value is comparable to those of the CuO/TiO2 and Cu2O/ZnO catalysts. In addition, there is still much room for improving the CO2 reduction activity and alcohol selectivity of the desired Cu2O-o catalyst, and this deserves more efforts in our future work. Overall, the Cu2O-o catalyst with good ECR performance shows promise for CO2 reduction application.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In summary, we have synthesized Cu2O nanostructures with tunable crystal facets via a hydrothermal process. The electrochemical CO2 reduction performance of the assynthesized Cu2O catalysts has been investigated. Our results indicate that the catalytic activity and alcohol selectivity of the Cu2O catalysts depend on the exposed different crystal facets. The desired Cu2O-o catalyst enclosed with (111) crystal facets exhibits good electrochemical performance with a high partial current density of −0.51 mA/cm2 and a great selectivity of 35.4% toward alcohol production under −0.3 V vs RHE. In addition, the desired Cu2O catalyst shows good stability in the long-term CO2 reduction test. The good electrochemical CO2 reduction performance is associated with the facet-dependent effects. The Cu2O catalyst enclosed with (111) facets contains enriched oxygen-vacancy defects for lowering the rate-limiting activation barrier and facilitating CO2 activation. The (111) facets are conducive to reducing the energy barrier for C−C coupling and transformation of the key intermediates and promoting electron migration for enhanced alcohol production. In addition, the short Cu−O bond on (111) facets of Cu2O-o endows the catalyst with a lower kinetic barrier to be overcome and therefore affords the sample a facilitated CO2 reduction process. Surface reconstruction of the Cu2O catalysts also contributes to the enhanced ECR performance, with respect to the synergistic roles of Cu0 and Cu+ sites in promoting CO2 activation and stabilizing CO* adsorption for boosted C−C coupling. Our findings have provided insights into enhancing the ECR performance of Cu2O nanostructures by crystal facet engineering. More efforts will be devoted to tuning the particle size and boosting the concentration of oxygen-vacancy defects to further improve the reduction activity and alcohol selectivity of the desired Cu2O-o catalyst.
